title: Terumah: willing hearts (Exodus 25:2)
hookLine: the sanctuary is built only from gifts "of every man whose heart maketh him willing"

lines: A GIFT CARD, A LOPSIDED MUG.
A SANCTUARY, AND WHERE IT COMES FROM.
cards: Two gifts arrive in the same week. One is a gift card from a relative who was reminded to send something, with a printed signature.
The other is a mug from a child, lopsided, thick with paint and glue, handed over with both hands. One cost more. Only one was made because someone wanted to make it.
God is about to ask the people to build a sanctuary in the wilderness, a dwelling place for the divine presence. It will need gold, silver, fabric, wood, oil.
And the very first instruction is about where all of it is allowed to come from.

teach.h: THAT THEY TAKE FOR ME AN OFFERING.
teach.b: The portion is called Terumah, and it begins, in the old Jewish translation: "Speak unto the children of Israel, that they take for Me an offering; of every man whose heart maketh him willing ye shall take My offering."
Terumah is the Hebrew word for that offering.
Its root means to lift up, to raise: something you lift out of what you have and set apart, the way you might lift the best piece onto someone else's plate.

Then the list: gold, silver and copper; blue, purple and scarlet wool; fine linen and goats' hair; rams' skins dyed red; acacia wood; oil for the light; spices for the anointing oil and incense; onyx and other stones.
But notice the condition. Not a tax. Not a quota.

Only from every person whose heart moves them; the Hebrew is literally whose heart makes him willing, or urges him on. Readers have noticed something else in the first line. It says take for me an offering, not give.
Some Hasidic teachers liked to say that when you give from the heart, you're also taking: you receive something by giving. Whether or not you read it that way, the point of the opening is plain.
A house for God built from forced gifts wouldn't be the house the Torah has in mind.
It has to start with willing hearts.

how: In Jewish life, giving is both a duty and a gift: tzedakah is expected of everyone, and alongside it Jews also give freely to synagogues and causes, often recalling that the sanctuary was built from gifts of willing hearts.

games.q: you're raising materials for a house for God in the wilderness. what does the first instruction say?
o: collect a set amount from every family.
take from every person whose heart makes them willing.
games.why: only willing hearts. not a tax, not a quota. the house starts with gifts given freely.

practice: Set aside what you should give, or what's expected, and ask what you'd actually like to lift out of your life and offer: some time, a skill, an object someone else would love, a compliment you've been holding back.
Let something come up that feels light to give, not heavy, and notice the difference between should and want to.
